#3336. IEEE Offers More Services to Cities That Want to Be Smarter

They include webinars, educational resources, and conferences

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

More and more city governments are using advanced technologies to improve livability for their residents. Municipalities use data from smartphones and sensors for traffic enforcement, traffic control, and waste management. They also have implemented artificial intelligence and deep learning programs.

Dubai, Paris, and Coral Gables, Fla., are among the cities that have invested heavily in programs to become smarter.

Although many initiatives have delivered real innovations, not all have been successful. Inefficient global coordination has hindered projects with unclear standards, socioeconomic differences, and a lack of worldwide governance, leading to a disconnect between the technologies and the ability to adapt to them.

Smart city projects are complex and expensive endeavors that involve politicians, citizens, technocrats, and engineers. Successful projects require citizens to be fully engaged and to have strong collaborations with the participants, especially engineers, as engineering is the cornerstone.

Collaboration with universities, research institutions, and technology experts can bridge knowledge gaps on the behavior of complex socio-technical systems. What’s missing, though, is a global platform where those involved can discuss their experiences.

To help solve those and other challenges, the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community (formerly the IEEE Smart Cities Initiative) was launched in 2013 by IEEE Future Directions, which incubates emerging technologies and new applications of current ones. The technical community provides city leaders and others with credible, unbiased information and educational content developed by IEEE experts.

Since then, IEEE Smart Cities has launched services including its flagship International Smart Cities Conference, a media center with educational and technical resources, and a contest to recognize the best smart project completed by city officials. The platforms bring together practicing engineers, academic researchers, policymakers, and city leaders to collaborate and exchange ideas and experiences about moving toward a smart-city model.

In 2021 the IEEE Power & Energy Society began managing the Smart Cities program, which is supported by the IEEE Communications, Industry Applications, and Intelligent Transportation Systems societies and other IEEE entities.

Thanks to volunteers’ dedication and determination, IEEE Smart Cities launched several services. But the initiative’s structure limited the development of long-term projects and the creation of new activities.

To address the situation, the IEEE Technical Activities Board (TAB) created the second-generation technical community ad hoc committee, also in 2021. It was a pilot program whereby IEEE Smart Cities formed a board of governors to oversee the community’s operations and leadership, and created a policies and procedures manual.

In November 2025 IEEE Smart Cities became a TAB technical community.

Today more than 7,000 volunteers collaborate on various aspects of the community within at least one of the following technical tracks:

New webinar series, workshops, conferences, educational resources, and other offerings are being created.

Two events were launched recently: the IEEE European Technology and Engineering Management Summit, held in May 2025 in Belgium, with the next one planned for 2027; and the IEEE Sustainable Smart Lighting World Conference, scheduled for 2 to 6 December in Athens.

The Smart Cities Ambassadors program aims to raise the technical community’s visibility outside IEEE by holding roundtables and other events at non-IEEE functions.

IEEE Smart Cities volunteers are working on launching journals. In addition, standards are being developed in collaboration with the IEEE Standards Association, societies, and councils.

The program is collaborating with the Open and Agile Smart Cities and Communities network, the Instituto de Competitividad e Innovación para el Desarrollo y Transferencia de Tecnología, and the International Project Management Association.

All of those actions have the ultimate objective of boosting IEEE Smart Cities’ growth and sustainability, as well as strengthening the leadership and educational offerings to technical community volunteers.

If you would like to volunteer, visit the Smart Cities website.

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

#3332. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

Thank you for pointing out this accessible opportunity. I wonder why the industrial and non-residential building sectors still haven’t implemented this technology on a broad scale. The variable frequency drive (VFD) technology is very mature, widely available, and not new. It’s such a low-hanging fruit to implement wherever there are rotating machines and actuators to save energy, money, and also make the whole integrated energy system potentially more flexible and efficient.

#3330. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3329. Linda Perry Let Her ‘Let It Die Here’ Director Document “One Long Meltdown” That Resulted In A New Song, And A Movie – Sound & Screen Film

In her Tribeca Festival documentary Linda Perry: Let It Die Here, Linda Perry fans were treated to a rare POV of the 4 Non Blondes frontwoman’s life and musical process.

At Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film, the five-time Grammy nominee performed “What Lies with You” from her fourth solo album Let It Die Here, and recounted writing the song after going through “one long meltdown” following her mother’s death, as well as letting director Don Hardy Jr. shoot a four-hour jam session where “the song came to life in the film” after she wrote it the night before.

“Don and I worked on a film called Citizen Penn for Sean Penn, and then we just kind of became friends, and he asked me, ‘You know, you’re super interesting. Can I just come in your studio and film your process?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah!’ And then, I thought I would just get some good Instagram content, because I’m terrible at it. I mean, swear to f*cking god,” Perry told the Sound & Screen audience.

“And then, as it always happens when a camera shows up, things start happening,” she added. “And I was struggling a lot, I was just having such a hard time figuring out how to write a song for myself.”

Perry continued, “And then Don came and said, ‘Hey, you know, the footage I’ve been shooting, I think there’s a documentary here. I’m seeing it kind of clear.’ And I was just like, ‘I don’t wanna hear about it. Don’t tell me about it. I don’t wanna f*cking know about it.’ And then, he’s like, ‘But you understand it would be about you?’ And I’m like, ‘I get it. If I said it, I said it. If I did it, i did it. But don’t bring it up to me.’ And that’s kind of how it happened.”

In Linda Perry: Let It Die Here, now available to stream on Hulu and Disney+, the artist provides an intimate look at her life, career and personal struggles.

Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and with Black Friday approaching, this 2026 model is already seeing a $500 discount, bringing its price down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date, according to price trackers.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

#3327. Report: Apple faces congressional scrutiny over ICE tracking apps and Trump donations

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

Reuters, meanwhile, reported that Senator Richard Blumenthal, “who is set to take over as chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations,” called on Apple “and others who donated to [President Trump’s new White House] ballroom project to turn over records” or “face possible subpoenas in January.”

As The Washington Post reported last month, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million toward the ballroom, making them two of the project’s largest donors.

Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters or The Washington Post.

You can read the full Reuters report here, and The Washington Post’s here.

Smart city deployments have historically relied on cameras, sensors, and dashboards that capture data without delivering timely insight. #3324. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

This week, Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left to make it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

#3323. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3322. Skydance Bosses Throw Shade On Warner Bros Film Slate; Q4 Profit Will Take $200M Hit

There’s a lot for Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz to be proud of in their purchase of Warner Bros.

As Ellison said Monday during Skydance’s Q3 earnings call, “We have approximately $40 billion [in film] franchises which I think highly strengthen the overall portfolio,” and that “a new movie will arrive on our service every other week; film is a major driver of acquisition and engagement on our platforms.”

Despite potential plusses from the merger, Ellison and Kreiz also drew attention to the losses in store from Warner Bros’ 2026 film slate.

More specifically, Ellison wasn’t shy in acknowledging that Paramount is in better financial waters going forward than Warner Bros on the feature side. Today’s earnings didn’t include the consolidated Warner Bros figures since the merger closed during Q4, just five weeks ago; still, Paramount brass painted a less-than-rosy picture of what’s around the corner. Watch on Deadline

Said Ellison at the call’s onset, “The 2026 Paramount film slate is expected to generate $500 million more in lifetime profits than last year’s. We’ve now taken on another company with mixed results across the business…”

“We’ve proven it works, and we’re confident it will work again,” Ellison said, as the company is still looking at $6 billion synergies from the merger.

Kreiz mentioned at the top of the call about the merger, “What I’ve seen, the various parts of the company are in strong shape. The Warner Bros. Discovery team did a good job managing their business and delivered the expected result through the close, with the one area of softness in the movie studio, and we are looking to build on their good work.”

Skydance CFO Dennis Cinelli drilled down further on the red ink from Warner Bros, which saw right before the merger closed a major bomb in the Tom Cruise-starring political satire Digger, which cost $160M before global P&A and yielded $50.3M in worldwide box office.

Cinelli said, “For the full year, Warner Bros is on track with our underwriting plan, with the exception of the near-term film slate. And Paramount remains on track for our 2026 guidance which is including the high-end of the profitability range at $3.9 billion adjusted EBIDTA.”

The CFO added, “While the Paramount film slate continues to perform well, that will be more than offset by the continue underpeofmance of the Warner Bros film slate. Based on this, we expect to have a $200M headwind to adjusted EBIDTA in Q4. That includes films already released quarter to date as well as films that we will release going forward.”

The $200M headwind is essentially Digger, more or less.

There was a report out there that Warner Bros’ 2026 slate was bound to lose $800M for the full year; we know from sources that is false. Even with the expected blockbuster success of Legendary’s upcoming Dune: Part Three, the WB slate is estimated to lose around $400M, per sources.

It hasn’t been a great year at the box office for Warner Bros, with global box office misfires such as Supergirl, The Bride, Digger and no film grossing more than $100M domestic. However, the Burbank lot is slightly ahead of Paramount at the domestic box office year to date, from January 1-November 9: $569M (-70% vs. same frame in 2025) to $537M (+15% vs. ’25). Combined, the two studios count $1.1 billion at the domestic box office YTD, ranking behind Universal ($1.9B), Disney ($1.6B) and Sony ($1.4B). Paramount’s high points have been Scream 7 ($121.9M domestic) and Scary Movie ($108.2M).

In a further sign to Wall Street that it is cutting fat, Skydance today announced the departures of prolific filmmakers James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios’ heads. They are being replaced by early-2000s Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham, who departed the Disney-owned studio in 2017 before the explosion of Black Panther, Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame.

Ellison wasn’t all poo-poo on Warner Bros today. He gave props to New Line’s upcoming 2027 Christmas event title Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum calling the movie, “a compelling theatrical offering.”

This is one of those rare opportunities that don't come very often in the consumer tech space: Right now, you can get a 65-inch OLED TV from Samsung for $899.99 (originally $2,099.99) from Best Buy during its early Black Friday sale. This 2026 TV is considered an "entry-level" OLED, but it's still an incredible value for the money and the lowest price it has ever reached, according to price-tracking tools. There's a catch, though: The deal expires tonight, Nov. 10, at 1:00 a.m. EST.

If you've never owned an OLED before, there are some things you need to know to make sure it's a good fit for you. Perhaps most important is that they don't get as bright as QLEDs or LED TVs. Since this is an entry-level OLED, it likewise won't reach as high brightness as more premium OLEDs. This makes it less suitable for viewing in very bright rooms. There is also no Dolby Vision support (though there is support for HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG). But that is where the cons stop.

The S84H offers the near-perfect black levels you can expect from any OLED TV, making the contrast look incredible. The pixel-level dimming and viewing angles are also on par with other high-end OLEDs, and this TV also offers great features for gamers, including 4K support at 120Hz across all of its HDMI 2.1 ports, a variable refresh rate, and auto low latency mode.

OLED TVs are not normally priced under $1,000, especially newer models like this one. It's an incredible value for the money. The last time a deal like this popped up was in February, and before that, last Christmas, but for the 2025 version of this TV. If you're reading this after the sale has ended, you'll likely see the deal again in the future—perhaps even next month.

#3318. Kris Bowers On Creating A Love Letter To Ghana & Film History With His Score For ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’ – Sound & Screen Film

“We wanted this score to be a love letter to Ghana and to the history of film,” Kris Bowers says of his work on The Eyes of Ghana, the latest feature from Canadian filmmaker Ben Proudfoot.

The Oscar-winning musician was speaking at Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film event, where a live orchestra performed parts of Bowers’ score.

Directed by Proudfoot, with Barack and Michelle Obama and content creator IShowSpeed on board as producers, The Eyes of Ghana spotlights Chris Hesse, the 93-year-old forgotten personal cinematographer of revolutionary African leader Kwame Nkrumah. The Eyes of Ghana details the rise and fall of Nkrumah, a towering figure of African history who served as Ghana’s first President and led decolonial efforts across the continent.

Nkrumah was toppled in 1966 by a CIA-orchestrated military coup. As a result, the films made during Nkrumah’s time were ordered to be burned. Hesse is the film’s unsung cinematic hero, along with his protégé, filmmaker and producer Anita Afonu. The documentary unveils a huge archive of surviving celluloid films from Africa’s liberation era in the 20th century, which were long thought to be destroyed but were quietly safeguarded by Hesse for more than 60 years.

Bowers and Proudfoot previously worked together on the 2023 short The Last Repair Shop, which won the Documentary Short Film Oscar in 2024. The musician said he became involved with The Eyes of Ghana after Proudfoot sent him a sizzle reel of the footage he was working with.

“I remember watching it in my car,” Bowers says. “After I finished watching it, I was filled with emotion just because of how much, as a Black man, my own history is lost. And it’s sad that at some point you have to give up. So, the idea that someone like Chris Hesse has preserved this history and a vision of people that look like me that I had never seen from that era made me feel incredibly moved.”

The Eyes of Ghana was produced by Breakwater Studios’ Proudfoot and Nana Adwoa Frimpong, Afonu, Bwayo and Brandon Somerhalder alongside Higher Ground’s Ethan Lewis and Vinnie Malhotra. Barack and Michelle Obama are executive producers.

The film was released as a one-night theatrical event across the U.S. and Canada on October 28. It is currently enjoying a sold-out run at DocHouse in London. The film also screened at the Dikan Center in Accra, Ghana.

#3317. Apple TV renews ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ for season three

Award-winning culinary show ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ is getting a third season, in an announcement that came hours after its second season came to a close. Here are the details.

Just as ‘Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook’ premiered with a two-episode combo, and ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ aired its second season finale, the company confirmed that the latter will return for an eight-episode third season.

‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ is hosted by Topjaw’s Jesse Burgess and executive produced by Gordon Ramsay. Each season tells the story of several restaurants around the world as they compete to earn, retain, or increase their Michelin Star ratings.

The show premiered on Apple TV in 2025 to a perfect 100% Tomatometer score and has since been nominated for a BAFTA Television Award in the Factual Entertainment category, and won Best Popular Factual Programme at the 2026 Broadcast Digital Awards.

With eight episodes in each season, the show has taken viewers inside some of the world’s most acclaimed restaurants, including Brazil’s Evvai, the first in Latin America to earn three Michelin Stars, and Ynyshir, a two-star restaurant in rural Wales.

“What I love most about making ‘Knife Edge’ is that, however much time I spend in restaurants around the world, I’m constantly surprised by the extraordinary people and stories we discover. Behind every restaurant is a very personal journey, and for the chefs we follow, a Michelin Star can represent years of sacrifice, obsession and an enormous amount of hard work. It’s a privilege to be able to tell these stories, and I’m absolutely thrilled that we get to do it all again for a third season”

#3316. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on DeWalt, Milwaukee, and Ryobi Cordless Power Tools

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

Becca has also written for Angi, where she specializes in creating guides for DIY, home maintenance, and renovations, and she indulges her love of sci-fi and fantasy by writing about entertainment and science for Giant Freakin Robot. She serves on the board of the Good Junk Sanctuary in Portland, Oregon, focusing on community engagement in the DIY and reuse space.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales on tools to wind down by December 2, 2026.

EXCLUSIVE: My Jesus film has added 6 new cast members, including Abby Glover, Sophia Bunnell, Chloé Flowers, Pilot Bunch, and Cheyenne Jackson. They join the previously announced cast, led by Aliza Kate Barlow: Gavin Casalegno, Monica Potter, Kay Oyegun, Beau Bridges, and Charles Esten.

Country singer Carly Pearce will make a special appearance in the project from Lionsgate and Kingdom Story Company, inspired by the Anne Wilson book My Jesus: From Heartache to Hope.

The music-driven, coming-of-age film follows the inspiring story of Anne (Barlow), a regular teenager who is driven by a life-altering moment to post a video of herself singing online, triggering an avalanche of responses and catching the attention of executives across the Christian and country music industries. But finding her voice means Anne must also navigate the impact her gift has on everyone around her, including the changes it brings to her family and friends and the weight of her own expectations. Along the way, she must redefine how she views herself, her place in the world, her relationship with God, and ultimately, her purpose. Glover will play Liz, Anne’s sister; Bunnell will play Emma, Anne’s friend; Flowers will play Carson, Anne’s friend; Bunch will play Wylie, Anne’s classmate; and Jackson will play Dan, general manager of the Grand Ole Opry. Watch on Deadline

Kay Oyegun will direct the film in her feature directorial debut and has also written the screenplay. Kingdom Story Company’s Joshua Walsh, Brandon Gregory, Andrew Erwin, and Daryl LeFever will produce, with Jim Miller, Matthew West, and Robert Deaton serving as executive producers, alongside Capitol Christian Music Group’s Brad O’Donnell and David Blackman. Meredith Wieck and Maria Ascanio are overseeing for Lionsgate. Gaby Ludlow at Kingdom Story Company and Phil Strina at Lionsgate negotiated the deals.

Glover is represented by Take 3 Talent Agency, Rebel Creative Group, and Vainshtein Law. Bunnell is repped by Paradigm Talent Agency and Circle Management + Production. Flowers is repped by Gersh and Luber Roklin. Bunch is represented by CESD, Formation Talent Agency and Thruline Entertainment. Jackson is represented by Buchwald, Entertainment 360, and Lichter, Grossman, Nichols, et al.

Following the redesign of the Apple Music app icon, which replaced the familiar white music note on a red background with a black-and-white look, Apple today updated Apple Music Classical to match the new design.

Today, Apple updated the Apple Music Classical app icon and interface to bring them in line with Apple Music’s new visual identity.

The new icon retains the familiar G-clef musical symbol, but now features a black symbol against a white background.

Interestingly, unlike the regular flat Apple Music icon, the Apple Music Classical icon kept its three-dimensional look, with subtle lighting, shading, and transparency that give it a sense of depth.

While many assumed Apple would eventually adopt the more colorful design as Apple Music’s new app icon, today’s Apple Music Classical update suggests that the company is sticking with the black-and-white look for its apps.

Skydance Games has lost a number of staffers over the last few days, making it the latest division to be slimmed down and restructured after the merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.

“As part of our ongoing efforts to position Skydance Games for long-term growth and success, we are implementing reorganization and operational shifts across a few areas of our business. We are committed to approaching the process with transparency, care and respect for those who are leaving the company.” Related Stories Executives Skydance Bosses Throw Shade On Warner Bros Film Slate; Q4 Profit Will Take $200M Hit News HBO Max-Paramount+ Bundle Set To Launch In Early 2027, David Ellison Confirms

It wasn’t immediately clear how many role were impacted or which projects are being scaled back. Watch on Deadline

Paramount Games Studio was created last summer by the merger of Skydance and Paramount gaming businesses and that in turn became Skydance Games after the merger with WBD closed Oct. 6.

The combined group is headed by president of Skydance games and experiences, Tony Driscoll, who previously worked with Fortnite. Late last month, Skydance launched a voluntary buyout program across the company as it shifted to a five-day-a-week in office policy. Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz have promised Wall Street at least $6 billion in cost synergies from the merger, which will include layoffs.

The duo earlier today presented their first quarterly earnings since the deal closed.

There’s been considerable consolidation in the games sector in recent years. Last month, Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to 25% of its workforce, including at the Xbox division.

#3308. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3306. Apple @ Work: Mac admins are shipping AI-written code with mistakes, but fixing the problems is taking days

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

There’s no doubt that AI tools are making IT admins faster at writing code, researching issues, etc. As a Mac admin, I’ve seen slow but steady growth in how I’ve used it in my daily work across all aspects of IT. It’s not perfect, though. I’ve used it to write scripts, troubleshoot networking errors, and more. A new report from Fleet puts numbers on the problem: it’s easy to ship things, but it’s hard to undo mistakes.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For this report, Fleet surveyed more than 250 enterprise IT folks who manage Apple, all with admin access to their device management systems. The folks responding to the survey manage an average of 2,000 devices, and nearly half have 6 to 10 years of Apple admin experience.

The debate over whether IT teams should use AI day-to-day is over. They already are, and in the past 30 days, 68% of those responding reported using AI for troubleshooting or log analysis, 62% used it to write scripts, and 61% used it to author device management profiles or configurations. The log analysis is something that I use AI for often. 86% allow AI-written output into production after some form of review, and only 14% keep it out of their production environments entirely. There simply is no world where IT can operate at the speed needed without AI tools.

69% of respondents can’t roll back a bad configuration change within an hour, and 43% need more than a day. Another 26% of those responding can recover the same day, but only by doing it by hand. This is the biggest red flag of the survey, in my opinion. AI lets you ship anything fast, but AI can ship bugs just like humans can.

Here’s a real scenario that can happen: an IT admin asks an AI assistant to write a configuration profile, takes a quick pass at it, and pushes it to a few thousand Macs in seconds. If something is wrong with it (a bad network setting, a restriction that locks people out of an app they need), unwinding it could take a while.

“Mac admins are basically engineers now, whether their job description calls them that or not.”

I agree with him, and I am somewhat not happy about it. The job of an Apple admin has moved a long way from deploying Macs and iPads and managing through a device management console. Today it’s identity, security, compliance, and app lifecycle, all on top of a macOS release that forces changes every year. IT teams keep getting more and more added to them without additional resources or taking things away.

31% said keeping up with Apple’s release cadence is their single biggest IT challenge, far ahead of everything else on the survey. On the bright side, Apple’s own management architecture is moving in the right direction. 53% already have declarative device management in production.

Apple has done a lot of work here, and it’s not even Apple that is to blame for the frustration. Apple has built the platform for IT to do everything it needs to do. It’s everything else. Security is harder. AI has made it harder. It’s the expectation that IT has to own AI while owning literally everything else.

IT is using AI to help with its work because it’s the only way to survive the onslaught of the AI era. You aren’t getting more help, but you’re expected to do more without anything being taken away from you. Even systems that don’t need as much day-to-day management as they did years ago, you still have to own and secure them. Hosted email is a good example here. Yes, 365 and Workspace have made it easier to keep email running. You aren’t managing servers as you did 20 years ago, but email is still not easy. You traded server management for AI-driven phishing scams, MFA management, and more. It’s two steps forward and one back. We need a period of three steps forward and zero back to get back to where IT needs to be.

You can read Fleet’s full Apple in the enterprise report on its website.

#3305. 40th Australian International Documentary Conference Announces First Group Of Speakers: Poh Si Teng, Tamara Kotevska, Basil Tsiokos & More

The Australian International Documentary Conference (AIDC) will be welcoming some of the top talents in the documentary field to its upcoming 40th edition.

Among the first speakers to be announced: Poh Si Teng, director of Oscar contender American Doctor and founder of Tiny Boxer Films; Oscar-nominated filmmaker Tamara Kotevska (The Tale of Silyan, Honeyland); Basil Tsiokos, senior programmer, Sundance Film Festival; Rachel Antell, co-founder of the Archival Producers Alliance; Mandy Chang, CEO of Documentary Film Council, and Darren Dale, managing director and producer, Blackfella Films. Related Stories Podcast Doc Talk Podcast Goes Live With Director Poh Si Teng And Physicians Of 'American Doctor' Documentary 'American Doctor' Unveils Trailer, Sets Theatrical Release Date; Award-Winning Film Follows U.S. Physicians Who Treated Children Badly Wounded In Gaza

AIDC, which describes itself as “the Southern Hemisphere’s premier industry event for documentary and factual storytelling,” will unfold from March 8-11 in Sydney – the first time the conference has been held in the capital of New South Wales in more than 30 years. An online marketplace follows, running from March 23-24. Watch on Deadline

The conference also announced its theme for 2027: Reframed, which AIDC says “invites us to look at the same realities through different lenses: to ask who gets to frame the truth, and what happens when we challenge the narratives through which accepted points of view have been historically understood.

“Through guest speakers and sessions, Reframed will call into question selective reframing through propaganda, misinformation, censorship and distorted realities, and will prompt us to harness alternate ways of seeing an existing truth through a contemporary lens by bringing in new, different and multiple viewpoints.”

AIDC notes the 2027 edition of the conference offers the opportunity to “look back in order to look forward, acknowledging that our understanding of the world is never fixed and ever changing. Reframed asks us to reconsider what we think we know: to reveal what has been hidden, challenge what has been accepted, restore voices that have been silenced, and shine a light on what previous frames have left out.”

In a statement, AIDC CEO and creative director Natasha Gadd said, “Celebrating our 40th anniversary as we embark on a new era, AIDC 2027 will be an essential gathering place for the documentary and factual sector to showcase not only what our diverse and creative storytelling community continues to create but to also actively reframe what the future could hold through bold thinking, innovative practice and radical solutions to complex sector challenges.”

Gadd continued, “Through our 2027 theme, Reframed, AIDC provides a vital forum to explore and interrogate who gets to frame the truth, the forces that shape our understanding of reality, and to consider what becomes visible when we change the frame.”

AIDC’s move to Sydney has been made possible by a new Principal Partnership with the government of New South Wales through Screen NSW.

“Screen NSW is proud to support the return of AIDC to NSW for its landmark 40th anniversary edition,” commented Screen NSW executive director Kylie Munnich. “With a packed line-up of compelling speakers and sessions, AIDC is set to bring together the best minds in documentary filmmaking, commissioning and financing from around the world.

“We’re excited to see Sydney become a hub for discussion and collaboration, reinforcing NSW’s position as a leading destination for the screen industry. We’re also delighted to present the FACTory International Pitching Forum, which continues to connect talented creators with decision makers and to champion bold new documentary projects.”

More than 750 Australian and international delegates attended AIDC’s 2026 edition. The organization announced a group of decision makers attending for the first time in 2027 along with companies new to AIDC’s market. In addition to Basil Tsiokos of the Sundance Film Festival, 2027 participants include Howard Myers-Rifai, Head of Unscripted Originals, Foxtel/Binge (Australia); Denise Barren, Assistant Director, The Whickers (UK); Aleksandra Derewienko, Head of Sales, CAT&Docs (France); Jane Nice, Head of Development, Icon Entertainment (Australia); Cynthia Paribello, Development Coordinator, Original Content, ESPN (USA), and Caden Pearson, Commissioning Editor, NITV (Australia), with more to be confirmed.

Returning commissioners and funders from high profile companies in the doc and factual space include Zoe Stinson, Acquisitions and Productions Manager, TVF International (UK); Pamela Martínez, CEO/Managing Director, Limonero Films (Spain); Bo Zhang, Head of International Department – Factual, bilibili (China); Jessie Shih, Director of Program Development, PTS | Taiwan Plus (Taiwan); Choy Lin Mok, Commissioning Editor, TRT World (Turkiye); Kazz Basma, Head of Sales & Acquisitions, Sideways Film (Spain), and Paul Wiegard, Co-Founder and CEO, Madman Entertainment (Australia).

These are additional program announcements made by AIDC for its 40th edition:

AIDC’s 2027 Marketplace & Industry Development Program will once again provide an expansive range of business and development opportunities specifically for documentary and factual practitioners.

Alongside sales, acquisitions, and funding decisions resulting from AIDC marketplace activity, in the past seven years, AIDC’s industry development initiatives have unlocked over $3.6 million in professional and project development opportunities, and awards and prizes.

Confirmed AIDC Marketplace attendees include representatives from high-profile broadcasters, streamers, distributors, sales agents and funding bodies like: ABC (Australia), BBC Storyville (UK), bilibili (China), Boardwalk Pictures (USA/Australia), Cargo Film & Releasing (USA), CAT&Docs (France), DMZ Docs (South Korea), DocPlay (Australia), Documentary Australia (Australia), ESPN (USA), Foxtel/Binge (Australia), Icon Entertainment (Australia), In-Docs | Docs By The Sea (Indonesia), Jambika Docs (Spain), Limonero Films (Spain), Madman Entertainment (Australia), NITV (Australia), Paramount ANZ (Australia), PTS | Taiwan Plus (Taiwan), SBS (Australia), Shark Island Foundation (Australia), Sideways Film (Spain), Sundance Film Festival (USA), The Post Lounge Group (Australia), TRT World (Türkiye), TVF International (UK), The Whickers (UK).

The 12th edition of AIDC’s market centerpiece, The FACTory International Pitching Forum, presented by Screen NSW, is currentlyaccepting submissions, with projects sought across three strands; theCentral Showcase (for projects in development with internationalpotential); New Talent Showcase (for projects by filmmakers presentingtheir first major work); and Rough Cut Showcase (for projects seekingsales, distribution, and exhibition opportunities). Selected projects willpitch live to decision makers during AIDC 2027, and also compete for seveninternational pitch prizes from festivals and markets, including SheffieldDocFest (UK), Visions du Réel (Switzerland), Doc Edge (New Zealand),Docs by the Sea (Indonesia), DMZ Docs (South Korea), Tokyo Docs(Japan) and Hot Docs (Canada). The final submission deadline is Sunday, 8November.

Meetings between industry guests and accredited producers will again take place through Cut to the Chase, AIDC’s curated meetings program for Business Pass and All Access Pass-holders. Now open for submissions, Cut to the Chase matches producers and their projects to the most relevant commissioning editors, acquisitions executives, distributors, sales agents, financiers and funders, with meetings with local and international decision makers participating in person taking place during AIDC and additional international meetings arranged online.

Returning for its fourth year is AIDC’s slate-pitching program The Showroom, designed specifically for established Australian production companies with multiple non-fiction projects in development. The Showroom generates business opportunities through extended meetings and exclusive access to high-level buyers representing international broadcasters, streamers and sales agents attending AIDC. Applications open 18 November.

The AIDC 2027 Marketplace & Industry Development program will also host a number of partnered initiatives, including the fifth year of the $100,000 Shark Island Foundation Feature Docs Pitch, offering up to four projects a $25,000 development grant and the opportunity to participate in the Shark Island Kangaroo Valley Development Lab; The Post Lounge Group Doc Pitch, with selected projects sharing in up to $35,000 of equity investment through development, production, and post-production support; and the $20,000 DocPlay Indie Booster, providing two independent feature documentaries at any stage, from development to completion, with up to $10,000 per project to boost their theatrical screening campaigns. Pitch meetings for each initiative take place as part of Cut to the Chase.

AIDC’s philanthropically-funded program for emerging and diverse storytellers – Leading Lights – will also return for its 10th anniversary edition, featuring a tailored professional development program and the exclusive Leading Lights Pitch co-presented by AFTRS. Applications for Leading Lights are accepted until 6 December, with successful recipients receiving a complimentary AIDC 2027 Sessions Pass.

Set to close AIDC 2027 on Thursday 11 March 2027, entries are currently sought for the prestigious 7th annual AIDC Awards, recognizing outstanding completed works of new Australian documentary and factual content across a refreshed seven categories: Best Feature Documentary, Best Documentary Series, Best Factual Series, Best Documentary/Factual Single, Best Short Documentary, Best Audio Documentary and Best Digital First Documentary. Submissions close Sunday 22 November, with late submissions accepted until Wednesday 25 November (late fee applies).

AIDC members will also soon be able to nominate Australian industry professionals for the fourth annual AIDC Southern Light Award, a $5,000 cash prize given by AIDC to an Australian documentary and factual industry luminary for their outstanding contribution to the sector. Opening date to be announced soon.

Between AIDC’s combined Marketplace, Industry Development and Awards programs, AIDC 2027 has already unlocked access to over $275,000 in project development funding, professional development and prizes for delegates. Further announcements about AIDC’s Indigenous Creators Program and major new initiatives and pitching opportunities will follow in the coming weeks, with the full session program to be revealed 2 February 2027.

#3304. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.
